items.summary: In a Nov. 24, 2026 opinion piece titled "Welcome to the Trump-Nvidia-China-AI Hyper-Spectacle," Graham Webster argues that the Jensen Huang–Nvidia affair has been fused into an overwhelming conflation of disparate issues by commentators ranging from social media figures to national security analysts. The article notes events cited as part of this agglomeration include Trump reinstating Huang as Nvidia's CEO, a meeting between Trump and China's Xi Jinping, reports that US officials believed a woman connected to Huang may have worked for Chinese intelligence, AI and corruption emerging among top issues in the election, Trump buying Nvidia shares, Huang accompanying an earlier trip to meet Xi, officials reportedly warning Trump that Huang may be compromised by Beijing, weakened US AI chip controls on China under Trump, Huang advocating selling chips to China, Biden-era chip restrictions, and concerns about Chinese leadership in AI. Webster attributes these events as reported or alleged sources rather than verified fact, pointing readers to exhaustive timelines from The New York Times—which he says broke the Nvidia scandal—as well as the Wall Street Journal, TechCrunch, and The Guardian. Drawing on Guy Debord's 1967 concept of "The Society of the Spectacle," Webster contends that bundling these themes into a single spectacle obscures empirical questions such as whether billions in smuggled semiconductors represent a dire national security threat or simply export-control violations with possible Trump administration complicity. He identifies five challenges: uncertainty about AI's transformative power and Nvidia's essential role; the chain of assumptions linking Chinese chip access to existential US danger, each independently questionable; conflation of AI issues with partisan politics, rule-of-law concerns, and money in politics; misleading jumbling within AI questions themselves regarding data centers, fossil fuels, LLM governance, catastrophic risk, and harms; and the importance of the specifics of Huang's alleged affair. Webster warns that congressional investigators may invoke everything from spy-sex to existential risk for viral effect, though he hopes legal process will restore a "political life directly lived."
items.title: Commentary Frames Nvidia-Trump-China-AI Scandal as 'Hyper-Spectacle'

items.summary: In a landmark US trial lasting two months, Huawei was found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, while being acquitted of the more serious overarching racketeering charge. The case centered on prosecutors' allegations that the Chinese technology giant engaged in lying, cheating, and stealing to gain competitive advantage. Jurors in Brooklyn court convicted Huawei of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions. However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of racketeering conspiracy, a charge requiring members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise. Federal prosecutors first announced charges against Huawei in 2019, following the late-2018 arrest of senior executive Meng Wanzhou (Cathy Meng) in Canada; she was held for three years before being released through a deal with US prosecutors. During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors that Huawei spent 20 years expanding its business by lying to banks about dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms. US Attorney General Todd Blanche stated in a statement attributed to him that 'For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft,' adding that those engaged in criminal activities would be held accountable through FBI and federal prosecutor work. In response, Huawei said the racketeering acquittal confirms allegations lack factual basis and vindicates its position over eight years. Defence attorney Brian Heberlig argued Huawei's business expansion across 170 countries with more than 200,000 staff resulted from hard work rather than criminality. Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified by the rejection of the racketeering charge but had mixed emotions about other counts; he said there will be significant advocacy to achieve the lowest sentence possible and fully expects Huawei to appeal through every available argument toward vindication. Sentencing is planned for September 2027.
items.title: Huawei Found Guilty of Stealing Trade Secrets but Acquitted of Racketeering

items.summary:
After embattled former Nvidia head Jensen Huang was reinstated and the company's stock surged, President Donald Trump took a public victory lap on CNBC, saying "I made the deal." He followed this with an AI-generated image depicting Huang surrounded by Secret Service guards in front of an Nvidia banner. The post underscored how closely linked Huang's fate now is to Trump's political fortunes.

While Trump says federal officials exonerated Huang and his reinstatement poses no national security threat, Democrats and some Republicans are promising their own oversight with subpoenas and compelled testimony to assess whether China accessed advanced microchip technology through Nvidia. Republican Senator Tom Cotton posted that "Congress has much to investigate." Any new revelations could damage both the company and Trump.

Huang faces a harsher spotlight despite his record of success, as he is free from criminal liability but under intense scrutiny. Trump also appears on the wrong side of public opinion regarding AI broadly; midterm candidates campaigned on restricting data center construction, California Democrat Sydney Kamlager-Dove criticized the administration for being "asleep at the wheel," and rural conservatives resent big tech demands.

The intervention exposed rifts in Trump's own administration between Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a China hawk, and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, an AI proponent, who feuded over new export restrictions. Polling indicated political corruption was a top voter issue this year, with former adviser Steve Bannon saying the government "bent the rule" to allow Huang's return.

Trump views economic success as central to his legacy and sees AI investment as fueling recent growth; he scolded states blocking data center construction and predicted that whoever wins the AI race controls world fate. He has become one of the industry's biggest boosters, rebranding it "super intelligence."
items.title: Trump's Nvidia Intervention Ties His Political Fortunes to the AI Boom

items.summary: The Nvidia board unanimously voted Monday to rehire Jensen Huang as president, CEO and fellow director just days after accepting his resignation over an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The announcement stated the decision followed discussions with Huang and input from senior U.S. government levels; President Donald Trump said he believed his intervention was crucial to the reinstatement. Just six days earlier, board members had unanimously accepted Huang's resignation following his admission about the relationship. Kathleen Day, a lecturer at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School, called it crazy for Nvidia Chairman Harvey Jones and others to bow to pressure over someone who hurt the company's reputation, emphasizing that boards should represent shareholders rather than the CEO. Corporate governance experts noted long tenures can compromise independence under New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq rules requiring majorities of independent directors; University of Reading professor Nada Kakabadse suggested board members should serve a maximum of eight years to maintain independence. Peter Cohan, an associate professor at Babson College, argued that by giving in to Trump the board endangered the company because Huang would learn he can act without consequences. Daniel Kinderman, a political science professor at University of Delaware, called it crony capitalism and warned it could open doors for more aggressive actions from elected representatives toward businesses. The reinstatement has renewed congressional interest around export controls related to Huang's affair raising questions about Nvidia's compliance; Democratic Senator Elizabeth Warren called the decision reckless while noting Huang, executives and the board still owe Congress answers, and Senator Kirsten Gillibrand demanded both testify publicly because a boardroom vote does not resolve a national security risk. California Attorney General Rob Bonta said Tuesday in an interview with CNBC that Trump's intervention does not bode well for federal law enforcement without fear or favour, following a Thursday announcement from the California Department of Justice asking Nvidia whether its advanced chips or confidential information reached China and whether it misled investors and the public. The board includes Mark Stevens and Tench Coxe who joined in 1993 when Nvidia was founded as venture capitalists; Jones and Brooke Seawell are former Synopsys executives with Jones joining in 1993 and Seawell four years later; Stephen Neal, designated lead independent director, joined in 2019. Melissa Lora spent 31 years at Taco Bell before joining the board in 2023, Aarti Shah came from Eli Lilly in 2020, John Dabiri is a Caltech engineering professor added in 2020, Dawn Hudson was NFL's chief marketing officer and Pepsi-Cola North American CEO on the board since 2013, and Suzanne Nora Johnson joined as a Goldman Sachs vice chairman in July. None of the board members provided comment to The Associated Press.
items.title: Nvidia Board Reinstates Jensen Huang Amid Scrutiny Over Trump's Role

items.summary: A jury in Brooklyn federal court convicted Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei on Tuesday, finding the company guilty of 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced in a case that began in 2018. The verdict held against Huawei on charges including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, and conspiring to steal trade secrets from American companies. Separately, the jury acquitted Huawei of two remaining counts—conspiring to obstruct justice and racketeering conspiracy—the latter alleging the company operated as a criminal enterprise.
items.title: Huawei Convicted in U.S. Criminal Trial Over Iran Business and Trade Secrets

items.summary: A federal jury in Brooklyn found Huawei guilty on 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, while acquitting the company of racketeering conspiracy. The verdict came years after US authorities targeted Huawei over national security concerns and placed it on a trade blacklist that restricted its access to US technology following Meng Wanzhou's detention in Canada in December 2018. Prosecutors alleged that Huawei misled HSBC, Standard Chartered, and BNP Paribas about its business dealings in Iran so the company could move dollars across sanctions violations, with prosecutor Meredith Arfa telling jurors during closing argument that "after the media started questioning Huawei's operations in Iran, so did Huawei's banks." The case originated from Meng Wanzhou's secret indictment for allegedly misleading an HSBC banker about Huawei's Iran business; she fought extradition for nearly three years before entering a deferred prosecution agreement and returning to China with charges dropped. Prosecutors added new charges in 2020 alleging that Huawei conspired over two decades to steal trade secrets from US technology companies, presenting evidence of alleged source code theft from Cisco Systems routers, antenna technology theft from Quintel, access to a circuit board developed by CNEX through a hired professor, and incidents captured on video showing employees taking items from T-Mobile testing robots and photographing devices at Fujitsu booths. Prosecutors relied partly on a statement attached to Meng's deferred prosecution agreement in which she acknowledged that the company illegally conducted business in Iran, though she did not testify while an HSBC banker she met with in 2013 did take the stand. The defense argued that HSBC and other banks knew about Huawei's Iran business and were competing for it; lawyer Brian Heberlig accused prosecutors of "cherry-picking" a handful of disparate incidents to support their claim of a 20-year conspiracy, asserting instead that Huawei succeeded through hard work, innovation, and investment in research and development. The company has more than 200,000 employees and operates in approximately 170 countries.
items.title: US Convicts Huawei in Trial Over Iran Business

items.summary: The Reserve Bank of India has set a minimum ticket size of ₹1 crore at the time of issuance as well as at any subsequent transfers for securitisation notes, per a circular. The ticket size refers to the size of investment by a single investor. This move comes amid declining demand from banks, insurers, and pension funds for long-term sovereign debt, which has affected government borrowing; liquidity in the government bond market is limited to a few actively traded securities, according to officials at a recent seminar organised by the Primary Dealers' Association of India. The RBI has provided an exception for instruments with amortisation structures, allowing them to be traded at amortised value even if the investment size falls below ₹1 crore. Originators are mandated to ensure agreements with special purpose entities (SPEs) require arrangements with registrars, depositories and stock exchanges, wherever applicable, to enforce the minimum investment requirement.
items.title: RBI Sets Rs 1 Crore Minimum Ticket Size for Securitisation Notes

items.summary: In an exclusive interview with the New York Post, President Trump said he would pardon reinstalled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if necessary — describing a pardon as “always an option” and stating it likely wouldn't be needed. However, Trump expressed that he believes Huang should manage without one and told him to simply “tell the truth” when testifying before Congress next week. Trump added that Huang doesn't need to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights against self-incrimination during testimony scheduled for Tuesday before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and Thursday before a Senate Banking Committee hearing, though he noted Huang's lawyers would advise him on whether to plead the Fifth — which lawmakers had not yet confirmed. Lawmakers are expected to press Huang about Nvidia's chip exports to China, possible export-control violations, and national-security concerns; Louisiana Republican Sen. John Kennedy predicted Huang might invoke the Fifth amid potential criminal prosecution. Trump said he intervened in reinstating Huang 11 days after his resignation over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy named Alice Huang (no relation), having spoken to Nvidia's board members directly and indirectly about bringing him back. He argued that choosing the wrong successor could harm the country, stating replacing Huang would be “a terrible thing for our country in many ways.” Trump also said he gave assurances to the executive branch on Huang's behalf during the intervention. On Nvidia's strategic importance, Trump said its success is essential to keeping the United States ahead in artificial intelligence and that he was open to the company giving the American government an equity stake — noting Intel handed over 10 per cent of its value last year.

items.summary: A US jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud as it grew into one of the world's biggest suppliers of wireless telecommunications network equipment. However, jurors acquitted the company of the most serious charge it faced: engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy to steal intellectual property from American companies. The verdict followed a lengthy trial during which US prosecutors argued that Huawei repeatedly stole technological secrets from competitors and partners in the US and elsewhere. Huawei was also accused of doing business in countries subject to US sanctions, including Iran and North Korea, and making false statements to US government officials and banks as part of an effort to hide its misdeeds. Lawyers for the company said US investigators had used isolated episodes of wrongdoing by a few of Huawei's more than 200,000 employees to spin a false narrative about a grand conspiracy that didn't actually exist.
items.title: Huawei Convicted of Trade Secret Theft and Bank Fraud, Acquitted of Racketeering

items.summary: On Monday (Nov. 23), Nvidia announced the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive officer, just over a week after his resignation; the board stated it had received input from senior levels of the U.S. government during its decision-making process. President Donald Trump posted on Truth Social that the country needs Huang's leadership for NVIDIA and the American economy to succeed and prosper, confirmed he spoke directly with Nvidia's board, and said he believed his intervention was very important. The announcement coincided with a reported US$1 trillion valuation gain, which Citi analyst Atif Malik attributed to restored continuity across Nvidia's product roadmap, customer relationships, and supplier partnerships, along with lowered leadership risk that had contributed to recent multiple compression; the article notes investors appear unconcerned about Trump playing kingmaker for two U.S. chip giants—having intervened in Intel last summer—and Huang's extramarital affairs with subordinates and a suspected Chinese spy. The piece argues business as usual would be a grave mistake, pointing to congressional appearances including Huang's scheduled Dec. 3 testimony before the Senate Banking Committee, an SEC investigation into accounting practices per Reuters, and Senator Chuck Schumer's statement that Democrats will investigate wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other NVIDIA executives, and anyone selling out national security for financial gain; Nvidia stressed its internal investigation would continue while noting a newly formed National Security and Export Control Committee comprised solely of independent directors. The article contends that had Huang suffered an accident rather than misconduct, questions about whether a US$4 trillion company faced withering away and grave risks to American national security suggest the situation is untenable—an indictment of the governance he presided over—and concludes that in any sane world his misdeeds would have warranted dismissal or leave until facts were fully known.
items.title: Nvidia Reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO After Government Intervention

items.summary: A US jury in the Eastern District of New York found Chinese tech giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets and bank fraud but acquitted it of a more serious racketeering charge, following an 11-week trial that concluded Tuesday. The verdict comes after charges first announced by the US in January 2019 were later expanded; prosecutors told the jury at trial that Huawei leaders engaged in criminal conduct including lying to Congress and banks, violating sanctions, and interfering with the investigation, according to reports from the Associated Press. Huawei has denied any wrongdoing throughout, stating in a statement released Tuesday that the acquittal on racketeering "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis" and vindicates its position over eight years, while asserting the remaining charges are without legal or factual merit. In his closing argument, Huawei lawyer Brian Heberlig argued prosecutors relied on innuendo and out-of-context facts alongside testimony from former employees with personal grievances, noting much of the allegedly stolen material was publicly available; he said Huawei would appeal the convictions.

items.summary: Jensen Huang was rehired as CEO of Nvidia just 11 days after resigning, with the company's board citing unanimous input from senior levels of the US government. President Donald Trump declared in an interview that he had personally convinced them to bring Huang back, a claim made even though the company had ruled out his return only days earlier. The rehiring followed reports of extramarital affairs—one involving a woman linked by US intelligence to China's top spy agency—and allegations from the Wall Street Journal and New York Times about Huang belittling staff, including a senior executive who temporarily succeeded him as CEO. Nvidia's stock had fallen sharply after his November 12 resignation announcement: closing at $174 on November 11 before dropping to around $126 within eight days, knocking roughly $1.2 trillion off its market value and dragging down the wider US share market. On Huang's return day, shares surged 31% to $165, pushing Nvidia's valuation back up by nearly $1 trillion. The company's board said its decision came after government input; Trump went further in declaring he had convinced them. An economist argued that as an incentive-driven actor, Trump weighed four main factors: the economic impact of Nvidia's falling share price on the wider US stock market—Trump told reporters last week's AI selloff was probably a factor but emphasized long-term effects and said 'I made the deal'—a political incentive tied to his claim that markets perform well under him amid talk of an 'AI bubble,' as Nvidia lost about one-third of its market capitalization; personal incentives, with the Financial Times reporting Trump could have gained $1.3 million to $15 million from Monday's share surge based on disclosures showing he may have owned up to 370,000 shares at September 30; and his personal relationship with Huang, who reportedly takes AI advice from Trump significantly and rarely mentions AI downsides while Trump has shunned doomsday scenarios. The article notes that under Huang Nvidia became the central bank of AI through advanced chips and funding for cash-poor companies like Anthropic and OpenAI in a circular financing model, plus $228 billion in guarantees, leases and investments for data centre providers; interim CEO Colette Kress reportedly renegotiated an Ohio OpenAI proposal from $250 billion down to half that amount as a counterweight to Huang on risky financing. The piece argues that had someone other than Huang led the company, AI investment might have slowed with real-world impacts beyond the US including how quickly data centres expand worldwide; now back as CEO, Huang's incentives align with Trump's to promote AI while suppressing criticism and maintaining circular finance.
items.title: Nvidia Rehires Jensen Huang After Trump Intervention

items.summary: The Nasdaq Composite and S&P 500 closed lower on Nov 24 as Nvidia and other AI-related shares gave back some of the previous day's sharp gains, with investors bracing for possible new tariffs. Nvidia's stock slipped 5.9% after Jensen Huang's reinstatement as CEO was confirmed on Nov 23 following questions about political and governance risks surrounding his return; Huang had resigned earlier in November over revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. Technology fell 2.8%, leading sector declines in the S&P 500, while a semiconductor index dropped 7.9%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 423.39 points, or 0.85%, to 50,018.70; the S&P 500 lost 36.08 points, or 0.50%, to 7,201.09; and the Nasdaq Composite fell 356.02 points, or 1.48%, to 23,733.54. Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group, said profit-taking was expected after the biggest rally in months but that one headline does not resolve investor questions about the AI trade and warned of a bumpy path ahead for long-term investors despite viewing last week's correction as a buying opportunity.
items.title: Nasdaq and S&P 500 Slip After Nvidia-Fuelled Rally

items.summary: Jensen Huang addressed Nvidia employees during an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, one day after his reinstatement as the company's chief executive officer. Speaking at the firm's headquarters in Santa Clara, California, he apologized for letting staff down and described the gathering as the hardest company meeting he had ever conducted. According to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified about a private internal meeting, Huang said he was in daily therapy to address behavior that led to his brief ouster from the top job, acknowledged violating Nvidia's code of conduct, and expressed gratitude for having a second chance to lead the company he co-founded three decades ago. The people also reported that Huang insisted he had not been reinstated because he is a 'tech bro' above the law, emphasized that the board would hold him accountable going forward, and characterized his remarks as somber.
items.title: Nvidia's Jensen Huang Apologizes to Staff, Discloses Daily Therapy

items.summary: Business academic Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale argued Monday that Jensen Huang's return as CEO and board member of Nvidia represents a mistake, characterizing the company as "a detriment to U.S. global industrial might" rather than its champion. He cited research suggesting Nvidia's most advanced chips have reached China despite export controls — including documentation showing Blackwell chips in China from an Israeli company called Lava three weeks prior, and that chips were channeled to Northwestern Polytechnical University for use in weapons funneled to Iran and Russia — as well as sinking shares of Anthropic, which he linked to the realization that China's open-source AI models such as Kimi and DeepSeek are "distilling" from top U.S. labs using high-end Nvidia chips, even though Nvidia has denied smuggling is a factor. Sonnenfeld noted Huang's reinstatement was greeted enthusiastically in Asia too, quoting The Washington Post's report of China's state-affiliated Star Market Daily headlining "The king is back!" He attributed the return to heavy pressure from Washington: after Nvidia's chairman had effectively ruled out Huang just weeks earlier, Vice President JD Vance led private weekend calls urging the board to welcome him back and President Trump called the board directly. Sonnenfeld said directors who agreed now face a "historic level of individual liability," pointing to five lawsuits filed in Northern California — an early class-action suit followed by a shareholder derivative suit alleging the board ignored red flags about Huang's relationship with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang, plus three more suits on Nov. 18 after Nvidia's most recent earnings call; he estimated around 30 costly suits could follow and cited 14 GOP senators who have come out against the move as factors behind Nvidia's tumbling stock. In a Q&A, Sonnenfeld said the board failed to rely on experts — including reversing course with Wachtell Law after it barely began its investigation — showed "incompetence and collaboration" alongside "cowardice in their capitulation," since less than 1% of Nvidia's business comes from U.S. government contracts compared with SpaceX's 46%, meaning Trump cannot threaten them as he might a company dependent on federal revenue; he also argued Huang was not essential to the chip designs (attributed to co-founder Chris Malachowsky and Jonah Alben) or CUDA software (Ian Buck), that his admitted extramarital affairs undermine enforceable conduct standards, and questioned whether Commerce will continue tightening export controls after partner Megaspeed landed on the U.S. trade blacklist Monday.
items.title: Yale's Sonnenfeld: Nvidia is a 'detriment' to U.S. industrial might — not a champion

items.summary: A US federal jury in Brooklyn, New York convicted Chinese technology company Huawei Technologies of conspiring to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks over its business dealings in Iran and alleged theft of American companies' technology. On Tuesday's verdict, the 12-count case spanning more than two decades resulted in convictions on 10 counts while jurors acquitted Huawei of criminal racketeering conspiracy, the most serious charge. The trial lasted more than two months after prosecutors called over 60 witnesses and defense attorney Brian Heberlig presented testimony from 15 witnesses. Huawei and three affiliates faced charges including bank fraud, wire fraud, sanctions violations, trade secret theft, and conspiracy to obstruct justice, with sentencing scheduled for next September where the company could face billions of dollars in penalties; no individual executives or employees were tried, according to a report by The Associated Press.

items.summary: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang opened his return to the company he co-founded with an all-hands meeting that addressed remorse, therapy, and the firm's code of conduct, according to multiple insiders who spoke to media. The succession planning issue also came up during the meeting; CNBC reported, citing an unnamed source present at the event, that Huang told staff Nvidia does not require succession planning because of its unique business model. He argued a succession plan would create unnecessary hierarchy, remarks seen as surprising given events over the previous two weeks when Huang resigned as CEO after admitting extramarital affairs with at least two people, including one whom U.S. authorities suspect is a Chinese spy. The company maintains a flat organizational structure unlike other large corporations; Nvidia has just five executive officers running operations—Huang, CFO Colette Kress (who served as interim CEO for 12 days), Ajay Puri of worldwide field operations, Debora Shoquist, EVP of operations, and Timothy Teter, EVP and general counsel, per the company's regulatory filings. Huang previously defended this structure in interviews, including a March conversation with podcaster Lex Fridman, stating that companies should focus on producing output rather than mirroring conventional organization charts. However, analysts noted his comments may not be sufficient to fully assuage the board or shareholders over the long term.
items.title: Jensen Huang Defends Nvidia's Flat Structure Against Succession Planning

The decline came as investor anxiety over artificial intelligence reasserted itself and optimism surrounding Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO waned. Huang's reinstatement had momentarily bolstered confidence in the AI trade and delivered a jolt that reverberated across global tech markets, but analysts said it was unlikely to fully resolve recent negativity. An analyst told the Financial Times that investors remain wary of supply-demand imbalances, regulatory risks facing the AI industry, and rising costs stemming from delays in data center construction. The analyst added that 'the recovery is likely to be limited, as the underlying conditions of the AI trade remain unchanged.'
items.title: Anthropic Shares Plunge as AI Trade Wobbles

items.summary:
On October 13, 2026, Meta announced its engineering deep dive into the new Facebook feature "Your Algorithm," which lets users express plain-language preferences for Feed and Reels. The item describes how large language models (LLMs) are embedded within a production recommender system, offering developers insight into explicit user preferences wired into an implicit-signal ranking stack.

The preference page has three parts: a one-sentence "Lately Summary" describing recent viewing; an "Interested In" list prefilled from past activity; and a "Not Interested In" list holding exclusions. Users can type interests, move items between lists, or delete them via the post's three-dot menu.

Meta frames the feature as addressing limitations of implicit engagement signals, which it says scale well but adapt slowly and miss nuance. The preference lifecycle runs on Meta's server-side ranking stack plus on-device cache invalidation in the Facebook app, split into four components: profile generation (an LLM turns refreshed interest signals into readable topic names and writes the summary), preference management (a smaller model checks coherence, detects duplicates, and maps phrases to clean topics), ranking (both lists apply across the funnel), and delivery optimization.

Validated interests are enriched with embeddings and search keywords, saved to a shared store read by both Feed and Reels, while a separate component runs integrity and safety checks. Each interest drives four retrieval sources: two match content directly through search and clusters of related topics; two extend reach via the content graph and item-to-item similarity. Passing candidates receive late-stage ranking promotion, then a reranking control layer prevents flooding by spacing out repeats, capping each interest's daily contribution, fetching one interest per request, and giving new interests temporary extra weight.

Exclusions use layered filtering at every stage: embedding comparison removes close matches, demotion rules push down near matches, and a fine-tuned LLM reranker reviews the final list. Quality requests such as less AI-generated or sexually suggestive content map to dedicated demotion signals rather than topic matching, while creator-naming requests filter that creator directly. On-device cache invalidation removes queued items before display.

Meta reports its small fine-tuned removal-list reranker beat a general-purpose model on speed and reliability, though it gives no latency figure for the supplementary tail load used to accelerate changes. The item notes Meta discloses zero metrics or model names, leaving claims unverified, and separately attributes conflicting reporting about custom-feed limits—YouTube's Help Center citing one feed versus TechCrunch reporting multiple feeds rolling out from October 2026—to those sources.

items.summary: Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive, reversing the board's decision to remove him in November amid a wave of negative reporting about his leadership. items.summary: At the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology earlier this month, MIT doctoral student Yunyi Zhu ’20, MEng ’21 — a CSAIL researcher advised by Associate Professor Stefanie Mueller — along with co-author Chang Xiao of Boston University, presented TangiMap, an agentic system that personalizes physical controls to help users “DJ their art.” The system maps digital widgets onto tangible inputs on everyday devices such as audio mixers and control pads, turning tasks like photo editing, sound mixing, 3D modeling, and character animation into more dynamic tactile experiences. Zhu described the broader vision behind TangiMap: using AI agents to adapt physical controls so users can interact with their devices eyes-free — adjusting a car’s volume without looking away from the road — or tweak multiple settings at once, such as brightness and contrast together while editing an image. The system relies on an AI agent that gathers context about the software being used, user tendencies, and the controlling device by drawing on sources including a program’s API, an MCP server, or a screenshot interpreted by a vision-language model; it then uses a large language model to compile this information into a file before mapping specific digital functions to physical controls. In demonstrations, TangiMap helped researchers reprogram a standard mixer as a photo-editing controller for Adobe Lightroom with on-screen visualizations of the controls, and similarly mapped sound-mixing software so performers can adjust music in real time using their own knobs and faders; it also adapted a simpler mixer to Blender’s 3D modeling program — including an area where users type prompts and then adjust features like shininess via physical controls — and connected specific expressions and movements to buttons on a control pad within Adobe Character Animator so users could animate or “puppeteer” a cartoon character live. The team created a custom user interface for each application, adding another layer of personalization while they hope to develop a more streamlined system that lets designers generate the UI by taking a picture; they are also considering physical aspects of interaction, such as using more ergonomic devices and accounting for where users position their hands during different tasks — noting people typically hold a mixer differently when making music than when playing a video game. Zhu plans a user study to gather feedback on TangiMap and whether this “smart DJing” improves creative experiences, while the dynamic reprogramming she envisions is more ambitious: physical items using an AI agent as a brain to decide what to reprogram into for a given situation — such as a chemical jar that could indicate when it’s sealed correctly or display its typical use on request. Their work was supported in part by Google’s Gemini Academic Program Award.
items.title: MIT Researchers Present TangiMap, an AI System That Repurposes Physical Controls for Creative Software

In an NPR interview, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a professor of leadership studies at Yale's School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, discussed what he called 'a new high - well, low watermark in American business history' following the board's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia's CEO after receiving a suggestion from President Donald Trump. Sonnenfeld described the board's judgment as worse than Enron or WorldCom and characterized it as 'a complete abdication of their responsibilities,' arguing that the directors were not sufficiently independent and instead capitulated to what he called 'the imperial will of the president.' He noted that less than 1% of Nvidia's business comes from government, in contrast to a hypothetical Starlink board where about 40% or 45% of revenues come from government. Sonnenfeld said this board should resign, comparing it unfavorably to boards that fired and later reinstated executives like Steve Jobs (whom he argued was 'a different' person upon return) and Sam Altman at OpenAI.

Sonnenfeld maintained that Huang's behavior had not changed, asserting that the alleged sexual relationships between a boss and subordinate constitute an ethical violation against Nvidia's code of ethics. He also raised concerns about sanctions evasion, stating that banned chips are being used in weapons design at what he identified as a military installation called Northwest Polytechnical Institute, with shipments going to Iran and Russia.

When asked whether Huang still deserved the Yale Legend in Leadership Award his school had given him last year, Sonnenfeld said no. He contrasted figures like Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, and Jeff Bezos—who have public 'quirky' or abusive sides—with Huang's previously perceived image as a congenial tech titan whose dark side was unknown to the public. Sonnenfeld noted that at Dell Technologies, Michael Dell suspected vendors in Singapore were diverting chips to China but stopped it immediately, whereas Nvidia continued such practices without anyone knowing about Huang's alleged conduct. He added that the board lacked any succession plan and had no one capable of stepping into the role.

items.summary: The text describes a paper presented at this year's International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) that applies physics-inspired optimal-transport methods to the multiagent pathfinding (MAPF) problem faced by Amazon Robotics, which operates over a million robots across more than 300 warehouses worldwide. MAPF requires collision-free coordination of robot movements in warehouse layouts modeled as W x H rectangular grids; at each time step a robot can move north, east, west, south, or wait, and finding optimal paths that minimize total cost without collisions is NP hard and computationally intractable even for moderate numbers of robots. The paper frames this challenge through the lens of optimal transport: Gaspard Monge's 1781 formulation sought to efficiently move resources from sources to destinations while minimizing cost such as distance or work, but his requirement that all mass at each source go to one destination created a difficult nonlinear optimization problem with potential combinatorial explosion. About 150 years later, Leonid Kantorovich relaxed this by allowing mass to split among multiple destinations, converting the problem into a linear program for which efficient algorithms exist; Kantorovich received the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for these contributions. The authors extend optimal transport using multimarginal optimal transport (MMOT), which represents robot locations at intermediate times so motion is modeled across both space and time. For anonymous MAPF problems, where any robot can go to any destination, they prove a key result involving total unimodularity (TU): TU guarantees that every corner of the feasible polyhedron has integer coordinates, so a linear program yields optimal and integer solutions in polynomial time rather than fractional ones like splitting half a robot across routes. At Amazon warehouse scale—a 150 x 150 grid with 1,125 robots producing 3.4 million decision variables over T = 30—TU-preserving MMOT finds optimal trajectories in 478 seconds versus the non-TU NP-hard formulation often failing to find a feasible solution in 12 hours. To address runtime concerns about accepting slightly suboptimal solutions, the authors introduce hot and cold gas models rooted in Erwin Schrödinger's 1931 work: lazy (cold) gas particles expend minimum effort for optimal paths equivalent to an optimal-transport problem but requiring long computation, while hot gas particles jitter randomly via Brownian motion for faster but potentially suboptimal trajectories; as temperature drops toward zero the hot-gas paths settle onto the lazy-gas ones. The authors model robot transport with a probabilistic Schrödinger bridge—an entropic relaxation of MMOT where added entropy controls trajectory randomness—extending fast Sinkhorn iterations to solve for shadows that reveal optimal path corridors, then recover integrality by removing decision variables where mass is small or travel unlikely. Looking ahead, the team plans extensions to labeled MAPF (fixed destinations) and lifelong MAPF (continuous task streams), combining linear and integer programs with learning-based approaches like DeepFleet and imitation learning.
items.title: Amazon Robotics and ICML Paper on Multiagent Pathfinding via Optimal Transport

In Part 1 of a two-part series, Databricks outlines the data modeling foundation needed to support customer decision-making by agents in an Agentic Customer Data Platform (CDP). The piece opens with a jacket price-drop scenario—where a saved item's price fell 30% nine days ago—to illustrate that whether an agent alerts a customer depends on goals and answers from six kinds of data. Databricks notes the data model is usually the hardest part for brands, positioning this guidance toward data architects who design stacks marketers and agents build upon.

Databricks states an Agentic CDP requires everything a traditional CDP needs—correct sources, clean data, one identity per customer, and trusted golden profiles—but changes in that agents take on more work such as matching records and drafting audiences while people choose sources, review matches, and approve outputs. Because an agent decides for one person in seconds, Databricks warns a gap in the data turns into a bad decision just as fast.

The company describes CustomerLake, built around defining trusted datasets and models once through Databricks and Unity Catalog so marketers can use purpose-built interfaces to ask questions, build segments, and activate audiences faster without working around IT or exporting data. The recommended flow is a medallion architecture with one rule: identity resolution runs after silver, and the canonical ID it creates becomes the join key for gold.

Databricks recommends building layers with Spark Declarative Pipelines, keeping them on schedule with Lakeflow Jobs, and governing every layer in Unity Catalog. It argues brands have long asked why they can't own their identity graph and run deterministic matching on their own data; Databricks says the usual answer was upkeep from rules, reruns, and reviews taking people and time, but with identity resolution running next to the data, owning the graph becomes practical—"in our experience it's the most important table you'll build."

The company describes its approach as Agentic Identity Resolution, combining deterministic matching (exact email, exact phone, a partner ID that maps to customer ID), probabilistic scoring of gaps, and LLM-based matching via Profile Agents for heavy lifting and golden-record survivorship, with manual data steward overrides allowing human judgment. It also advises keeping full consent history—one row per person, channel, purpose, source, and time—and suppressions like unsubscribes and bounces in silver to derive a 1:1 consent table; flagging each gold table for freshness; building event tables as streaming tables keyed to the canonical ID with continuous-mode pipelines for triggers like cart reminders while scheduled behavior stays batch until streamed; computing time windows against a declared as-of date so reruns give consistent answers; and keeping one governed copy giving each activation tool only the tables it needs.

Databricks states that once an audience or decision is defined on governed gold tables, it can be sent to channels customers use via CustomerLake's native Reverse ETL connectors syncing audiences and signals directly to martech, adtech, and CX channels without custom pipelines. It lists readiness questions for the foundation—including whether identity resolution runs in one place after silver before gold reruns as records arrive with a persistent canonical_id plus an auditable identity graph—and notes that if most can be answered yes, the foundation is ready for agents.

The series will continue in Part 2 by mapping B2C and B2B datasets onto the model; Databricks says it will return to the jacket use case to show which datasets answer each of the six questions.
items.title: Databricks Outlines Data Modeling Best Practices for an Agentic CDP

A Federal Reserve Bank of New York Liberty Street Economics post by Nina Boyarchenko and Leonardo Elias (November 24) examines whether the dramatic expansion of global corporate bond markets over the past three decades reflects a shift away from bank lending or simply greater overall borrowing. The authors note that as of end-2024, nonfinancial U.S. corporate bonds accounted for 29 percent of GDP, while in other advanced economies they averaged 11 percent of GDP. They argue this distinction matters because if growth comes from substituting away from banks, bond-market conditions govern a larger share of liabilities and bank lending standards a smaller one; but if firms borrow more broadly, the balance between markets is unchanged.

Documenting overall trends, nonfinancial corporate debt securities as a percentage of GDP rose in both regions. In the U.S., the market grew from 12.2 percent of GDP in 1950 to a peak of 36.2 percent in 2020—nearly tripling over seventy years. For an equal-weighted average of other advanced economies, bonds as a share of GDP more than doubled over twenty-four years, from 5.0 percent in 1996 to 12.2 percent in 2020; the authors note this size was partly inflated by pandemic-era issuance but that markets were growing steadily beforehand. Relative to GDP, bond market size then retreated between 2021 and 2024, mostly driven by outsized GDP growth.

Decomposing growth into changes in bonds as a share of total nonfinancial corporate debt versus credit deepening (total corporate debt relative to GDP), the authors find that before the pandemic most U.S. bond-market growth came from credit deepening: between 1996 and 2019, the market grew by 9.2 percent of GDP while total U.S. nonfinancial corporate credit rose from 41 percent to 52 percent of GDP—accounting for 6.6 percentage points—and the bond share climbed only modestly from 57 percent to 63 percent. Earlier (1980–1995), composition played a larger role, with more than 40 percent of the rise in bonds outstanding—from about 15 percent to 23.5 percent of GDP—due to firms transitioning from bank loans to market-based financing.

For other advanced economies as a whole, growth was a mix of both factors, but heterogeneity is substantial: while U.S. and Canada increases were mostly credit deepening, bond-market growth in New Zealand, Japan, and Italy came mainly from shifting debt composition toward bonds; France and Germany split roughly evenly (about half each), and the UK leaned about three-fifths toward credit deepening.

During the pandemic, bonds-to-GDP peaked in 2020–21. Decomposing growth between 2019 and 2021, credit deepened in sixteen of twenty-four sampled countries; for most Eurozone economies nonfinancial corporate debt shifted toward bonds, while for most other advanced economies—and the U.S.—the bond share declined as loans grew even faster than bonds.

On the post-pandemic retreat (2021–24), total credit to nonfinancial firms kept growing in nominal terms everywhere but GDP expanded more rapidly. In the U.S., corporate bonds rose from $8.0 trillion in 2021 to $8.6 trillion in 2024, while GDP grew from $23.7 trillion to $29.4 trillion over the same period. The authors find that although bond markets broadly declined relative to GDP—falling in seventeen of twenty-four economies—the source varied: in the U.S., UK, and Spain, faster-than-debt GDP growth meant reversal of credit deepening explained more than four-fifths of the decline (with bonds as a share of corporate debt actually rising in the UK and Spain), whereas in Sweden, France, and Austria a falling bond share accounted for most of it. Overall, the bond share fell in only half of sampled countries, so the retreat does not represent a broad-based return to bank credit.

The authors caution that conclusions depend on national accounts definitions—where the nonfinancial corporate sector boundary is drawn, whether bonds are valued at market or face value, and which instruments are included—and point to a companion Staff Report combining national accounts with instrument-level data for firms in more than forty countries. They also reference three related papers (a Staff Report plus two others) addressing how credit-boom composition affects the real economy, how much bond-market conditions matter per economy, and their effects on firm financing.
items.title: As Corporate Bond Markets Grow, Is Bank Lending Shrinking?

On Sunday, OpenAI chief scientist Jakub Pachocki published an essay titled 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' proposing that rival frontier AI labs agree on ways to slow the development of new models until adequate safety and monitoring tools are available. The essay disclosed for the first time an internal metric—log-perplexity—that tracks how much OpenAI's models improve during pretraining, inviting other labs to publish comparable numbers as a common basis for monitoring and potentially coordinating a slowdown.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman praised the essay on X, calling it 'the most important thing OpenAI has published in a while,' while Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman voiced his company's support and reported a progress score for one of its own models. However, Pachocki acknowledged that the proposal is unlikely to matter unless other labs publish their numbers and agree to speed limits; so far, Anthropic and Google DeepMind have not signaled willingness to sign on.

Pachocki cited alarming acceleration in AI advancement: OpenAI's progress score improved more in 2026 than in the previous three years combined, with an unreleased internal model showing another large stride. The published numbers are perplexity scores measuring how confidently a language model predicts the next word in unfamiliar text—lower scores indicate more confident predictions, and a log-perplexity of zero means assigning 100% probability to every correct token.

Since 2022, OpenAI's base-model log-perplexity has fallen from roughly 0.99 (capable of 'fluent conversation') to 0.76 (capable of solving 'a Millennium Prize math problem'). The chart's notable feature concerns what comes after current frontier models: GPT-6.2 Astra reaches a score of 0.76, while an unreleased internal model has already dropped to 0.73—a conspicuous break from the earlier pace of progress.
items.title: OpenAI's AI Progress Meter Aims to Encourage a Slowdown, But May Not Work

Speaking at the 5th India International Space Conference in Delhi, Narayanan explained that while Isro previously built PSLVs with industry support alone, an L&T and HAL consortium has now been given five PSLVs to build. NSIL signed a contract with the consortium in September 2022 for Rs 860 crore covering these five rockets. He said the first rocket is being prepared for launch by the first quarter of next year.

Narayanan added that Isro and INSPACe are hand-holding private companies to build many space assets for communication, navigation and earth observation, which he said cannot be done by the government sector alone; he projected benefits would appear five years from now. On Gaganyaan, Narayanan said it is not late but in its final phase as a technology-intensive activity, with the rocket and other items ready while work continues on the orbital module for launch at the earliest opportunity. One year after the US Department of Energy launched its Genesis Mission—a federal initiative to build an integrated quantum, AI, and high-performance computing platform for scientific discovery, energy innovation, and national security—the mission celebrated its first anniversary. The article was originally published in the Fall 2026 edition of Issues in Science and Technology and has since been reprinted to mark the occasion.

As a Genesis consortium member, IBM is contributing access to its hardware, software, and research across artificial intelligence and quantum computing, with plans by 2029 to deploy IBM Quantum Starling, the first fault-tolerant quantum computer capable of running a hundred-million quantum operations on 200 fault-tolerant qubits. In the past month alone, several initiatives advanced the mission's objectives: Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL), IBM, and AMD launched a co-design platform for quantum error correction combining IBM QPUs with AMD GPUs and CPUs; IBM deployed an IBM Quantum System Two with an Nighthawk r2 processor at the University of Chicago's Hyde Park Labs to support the National Quantum Algorithm Center; IBM and NVIDIA integrated the open-source Quantum Resource Management Interface (QRMI) with Slurm's Hierarchical Resources feature for quantum resource visibility in HPC workloads; IBM, NVIDIA, and Fermilab announced a modular quantum computing co-design platform for high-energy and nuclear physics problems; and IBM and AMD released Pelagos, an open-source framework that tests quantum error correction decoders against billions of simulated error patterns on GPUs.

IBM's involvement provides its ecosystem with new opportunities to advance quantum-centric supercomputing. The company installed an IBM Quantum System One at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in 2024 as part of the Curtis R. Priem Constellation and collaborates internationally, including running workflows across an IBM Quantum System Two and Japan's Fugaku system with the RIKEN Center for Computational Science. These collaborations informed a reference architecture describing how high-performance computing centers can co-locate quantum computers with next-generation classical systems using open software and standard interfaces.

As a member of Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Quantum Science Center—one of five research centers created by the National Quantum Initiative Act of 2018—IBM contributes to hybrid quantum-classical algorithms for materials simulation. In spring 2026, IBM, Cleveland Clinic, and RIKEN used quantum diagonalization methods to simulate a protein-ligand complex with over 12,000 atoms, the largest biologically meaningful molecular simulation performed with quantum hardware to date, using classical components on Fugaku and Japanese supercomputers. A project led by IBM researcher Kristan Temme that uses large language models to search scientific literature was selected for Genesis Mission's first request for applications.

In nuclear fusion work involving ORNL and a consortium of partners, researchers studied molten salts lining a tokamak reactor using up to 64 qubits and 2,654 two-qubit gates; AI agents analyzed 70 years' worth of experimental data on the materials. The Genesis Mission aims to accelerate scientific discovery by building a single compute framework combining hardware, software, and algorithms across classical, quantum, and AI domains.

IBM has been active in quantum computing since its inception: IBM fellow Charlie Bennett helped devise the mathematical basis for quantum computing, David DiVincenzo outlined five minimum requirements for creating a quantum computer while at IBM, and physicist Richard Feynman argued that nature simulations require quantum mechanics. IBM was among the first to put a quantum computer on cloud access; it has deployed over 90 systems and maintains processors with over 100 qubits capable of running up to 7,500 quantum operations each.
items.title: Genesis Mission Marks First Anniversary Amid Recent Quantum Computing Progress

items.summary: A Monash University study published in Science Advances analyzed 20 years of data (2000–2019) and found that an average of 916 million people—56% of the global population—were exposed on a single day to both wildfire haze and heatwaves annually. The number of co-exposed people increased by 287 million from one decade to the next, with the five countries worst affected being the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, Mexico, Brazil, and Russia. Researchers attributed this rise in concurrent exposure to climate change, which has increased the frequency and intensity of simultaneous heatwaves and landscape fires. The study was released in October 2025 while Indonesia battled wildfires described as its worst in 11 years; from January to Oct. 31, 2025, around 65,900 hot spots were detected—second only to the approximately 85,600 logged during the same period in 2015—and an independent assessment by The TreeMap estimated about 1.9 million hectares (4.7 million acres) of land across Indonesia was affected by fire between January and September 2026, 38% higher than its estimate for the same period in 2019.
items.title: Monash Study Finds Rising Global Coexposure to Wildfire Smoke and Heatwaves

Union Petroleum and Natural Gas Minister Hardeep Singh Puri attributed the stability to the Centre's strategy of cutting excise duties and managing domestic fuel supplies.

In New Delhi, petrol retailed at ₹102.12 per litre while diesel was priced at ₹95.20 per litre—the national capital maintaining relatively lower prices compared to other metros. Mumbai saw petrol at ₹111.21 per litre and diesel at ₹97.83 per litre. Chennai residents paid ₹107.76 for petrol and ₹99.55 for diesel. Kolkata had the highest petrol price among listed cities at ₹113.51 per litre, with diesel at ₹99.82. Bengaluru priced petrol at ₹110.44 per litre and diesel at ₹99.56. Hyderabad recorded the highest overall prices, with petrol at ₹116.15 per litre and diesel at ₹104.23.

Globally, oil prices steadied as traders balanced indications of rising supply against escalating attacks on vessels near the Strait of Hormuz, according to Bloomberg. Brent crude traded around $91 a barrel after climbing 2.3% in the previous session, while West Texas Intermediate hovered below $82. On Tuesday, Iran claimed a fourth tanker was struck by a mine, per Fars news agency, extending a recent wave of vessel attacks.

Tehran warned it would tighten its grip over the Strait of Hormuz until its demands were met, Tasnim reported—highlighting that an end to the nearly nine-month conflict remains out of reach. Even so, crude shipments from the Persian Gulf have surged in recent months, prompting the International Energy Agency (IEA) to forecast that the market will tip into a surplus this quarter.

Robert Yawger, director of the energy futures division at Mizuho Securities USA LLC, told Bloomberg: “The reality on the ground is more a ‘war but no war’ situation, with spasms of violence.” Under that scenario, he added, “look for the supply surplus to become the dominant theme in coming weeks.”

Brent has dropped sharply this month as Gulf exports climbed and US President Donald Trump held off on renewed strikes against Iran following the US midterm elections. Adding downward pressure, a key timespread for Middle East's Dubai crude benchmark flipped into a bearish structure this week, signalling that supply is now outpacing demand, per Bloomberg.

items.summary: An Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) report released Wednesday found a widespread culture of misogyny and sexualisation across NSW prisons, with Corrective Services NSW staff discouraged from making complaints. The commission identified a "boys' club" within the agency in which sexualised language was tolerated, citing examples such as female prison guards being called "split arses," a harassment complainant described by a senior officer as "demanding, a troublemaker and hysterical," and a probationary sexual assault victim told there "wasn't much that could be done." The report also documented a poor reporting culture and fear of reprisals, including an allegation that a woman forced to perform oral sex on a colleague was warned her life would become hell for reporting it. ICAC Commissioner Helen Murrell SC said the institutional failures compounded victims' trauma, stating Operation Targo "exposes an entrenched misogynistic culture across NSW prisons that tolerates harassment and abuse of staff while protecting alleged perpetrators." The investigation launched after 12 complaints about inadequate investigations into workplace sexual assault and harassment within Corrective Services NSW were received in late 2023 and early 2024, coinciding with a special ministerial inquiry into former prison officer Wayne Astill. ICAC conducted 14 interviews and six compulsory examinations but made no findings of corrupt conduct because the evidence did not meet the required threshold; lack of records and poor witness recollections also created barriers for investigators. The report acknowledged that complainants may be disappointed by the absence of adverse findings against individuals, while affirming there is "no acceptable reason why any complainant was silenced, unheard or belittled." ICAC made 10 recommendations to overhaul culture and improve accountability at Corrective Services NSW, including enhanced complaints handling processes, staff education, and a transparent process for reviewing investigations. Both Corrective Services NSW and the Department of Communities and Justice have accepted the recommendations.

items.summary: The U.S. Army's planned detonation of nearly 5 tons of unstable lead azide explosives on Wednesday morning near Middletown, southeast Iowa, will have long-lasting impacts on human health and the environment, experts warn (Inside Climate News). Even with mitigation measures such as blast containment walls and water misters in place, the controlled detonation of bomb-making materials is projected by the Army to release a toxic dust cloud that could travel over 100 miles to the southwest. There is no safe level of lead exposure; it can damage the brain, nervous system, and reproductive health and is particularly harmful to young children (Inside Climate News). Scientists and health professionals warn that lingering contamination after the detonation in air and soil could pose problems long after the blast for residents in the plume's path. Mary Jean Brown, a public health expert and former chief of the lead poisoning prevention branch at the CDC, said it is important to take this seriously and ensure children are not exposed (Inside Climate News). Following the planned 9 a.m. detonation Wednesday, airborne lead particles will likely travel southwest over the Missouri River and across Iowa's border into Missouri; the Iowa Department of Health and Human Services has advised residents in the plume's path to shelter in place for 24 to 48 hours after the blast (Inside Climate News). The Army is encouraging residents within an evacuation cone five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to leave the area for several days, with FEMA helping evacuate and shelter them through Friday, Nov. 27; Lee County Sheriff's Office issued a public notice Tuesday that soldiers will go door to door to notify residents (Inside Climate News). Evacuation is especially important for vulnerable residents including pregnant people or families with children under 6, Brown said, as lead can contribute to preterm labor, low birth weight, preeclampsia, neurocognitive and developmental delays, heart and kidney issues, and other problems (Inside Climate News). EPA officials wrote in a Tuesday news release that a controlled detonation during optimal weather conditions with robust mitigation measures significantly reduces the potential reach and concentration of lead dust landing on surfaces compared to an uncontrolled explosion. How far airborne lead particles travel will depend on their size and weather conditions; smaller particles may travel farther while heavier ones settle closer within days, and snow or rainfall can make lead settle more quickly (Inside Climate News). Nico Perdrial, associate professor of geoscience at the University of Vermont's Gund Institute for Environment, said although lead could remain airborne for a week or two after the explosion it will likely be diluted and spread out, but his biggest concern is that the explosion adds to environmental lead accumulation in soil over the long term. Gabriel Filippelli, biogeochemist and executive director of Indiana University's Environmental Resilience Institute, said low levels of lead occur naturally in soil but dust from the explosion and runoff could significantly raise those levels (Inside Climate News). Experts advise people within the plume's path to keep dust out of homes, wash hands and surfaces frequently, store shoes outside, wipe down all indoor surfaces with a wet rag even if windows were closed during the blast, wear an N95 mask outdoors for 72 hours after the explosion when cleaning cars or sidewalks, filter car air, avoid the plume's path while traveling over Thanksgiving, and test young children's blood lead levels routinely (Inside Climate News). Dr. Juanita Mora of the American Lung Association warned not to assume safety just because one is a few miles away since wind can bring dust near any area. Environmental monitoring before and after is critical; in addition to EPA and Army-led efforts, University of Iowa scientists including David Cwiertny are conducting independent sampling for transparency and public health (Inside Climate News). At a Tuesday press conference, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said the Department of Defense is investigating every weapon storage facility nationwide to ensure something like this never happens again.
items.title: Army Lead Blast in Iowa to Have Lasting Health Impacts

items.summary: According to the Technology and Engineering Center for Space Utilization of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, China and Pakistan will conduct four cooperative scientific experiments aboard the China Space Station. The Pakistani astronaut Muhammad Zeeshan Ali, who is set for a short-term flight on the station, will carry out related experimental operations in orbit, per Chen Mengyun, International Cooperation Project Manager at the center. One experiment, proposed by Pakistan's Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission, will examine how cyanobacteria grow and absorb carbon dioxide in space to provide data for future oxygen regeneration and biological production; the organisms used originate from Pakistan. Two materials experiments will test the protective performance of graphene-based composites and the repair efficiency of self-healing carbon fiber composites. Chinese and Pakistani scientific teams plan to jointly publish papers and share experimental results, Chen said. items.summary: India has made substantial progress reducing poverty: a World Bank report shows the share living in extreme poverty (below $3/day) fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, and those below $4.2/day dropped from 57.7% to 16.1%, with roughly 50 crore people escaping poverty overall. Yet the country still provides free foodgrains through the Public Distribution System (PDS) to more than half its population via the National Food Security Act (NFSA), which legally entitles up to 75% of rural and 50% of urban residents—about 81 crore people based on the 2011 Census—to subsidized grains, with beneficiaries receiving entitlements entirely free under PM Garib Kalyan Anna Yojana since January 2023 (5 kg per person or 35 kg per household). The broad coverage is justified by several factors: officials prefer over-inclusion to avoid missing genuinely needy families, following the Blackstone-era principle that it is better ten guilty persons escape than one innocent suffer; World Bank poverty measures rely on a single-period consumption snapshot and cannot capture transient poverty from job loss or medical expenses; removing ineligible households is politically costly since affected families are more likely to protest than the government celebrates savings; and free distribution provides a reliable outlet for procured grains, avoiding expensive excess stocks that could force procurement cuts hurting farmers in states like Punjab and Haryana. However, broad coverage also means well-off households—those with cars, air conditioners, three-plus-room homes, or government jobs—continue benefiting: a recent government-commissioned survey found about 13% of recipients were ineligible, exceeding 35% in West Bengal, Tripura, and Tamil Nadu. The financial burden falls on taxpayers through central allocation to states for distribution, diverting funds from infrastructure, employment generation, and other development needs.
items.title: Why India Distributes Free Rations Despite Falling Poverty

items.summary:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang apologized to employees at an all-hands meeting on Tuesday, saying he had let them down after the conduct that led to his brief ouster. According to people familiar with the matter who asked not to be identified because of the private nature of the internal gathering, Huang thanked CFO Colette Kress for leading the company during the nearly two-week period he was absent as CEO and described the meeting as “the hardest company meeting” he had ever held. He acknowledged violating Nvidia’s code of conduct, expressed gratitude for a second chance to lead the chipmaker he co-founded nearly three decades ago, and said he is in therapy daily.

Huang was reinstated on Monday following a pressure campaign by President Donald Trump after being ousted less than two weeks earlier over revelations that he had an affair with a subordinate and another relationship involving an alleged Chinese spy. At Tuesday’s meeting, Huang told staff the board brought him back because it evaluated the facts and was assured there was no threat to national security; he said his return was not due to Nvidia executives treating him as above the law or government pressure. He praised Trump as “my president,” saying he is in service of making the country successful, while adding that Nvidia is apolitical.

The meeting took place less than a week after an all-hands gathering proceeded without Huang following his ouster and board investigation into suspicions that someone connected to his relationship was gathering intelligence for China. Huang said the harder meeting had been with his wife. His reinstatement surprised most senior leaders, who had used last week’s event to demonstrate confidence in the company thriving without him.

Huang told staff he dislikes traditional succession planning because it can lead executives to fight over the top job; instead, he wants to keep a group of leaders at the same level focused on their areas of expertise. Videos shared by employees showed Huang returning to Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters Monday amid applause and cheers as he said in an entrance lobby address that he “will do a better job.” At Tuesday’s meeting, Huang did not take employee questions.

Nvidia shares rallied almost 31 per cent on the day of his comeback but fell more than 7 per cent in Tuesday trading. The company’s valuation is down close to $2 trillion from its October peak.
items.title: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Staff After Brief Ouster and Reinstatement

items.summary: On Wednesday (Nov. 25), Huawei rejected a U.S. conviction finding the Chinese tech giant guilty of stealing trade secrets, calling the verdict baseless and threatening legal action. In a statement released in Shanghai, Huawei said the charges are 'without legal or factual merit' and that it would 'thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests.' The conviction came from a New York federal court after a three-month trial, where jurors found the company guilty of 10 of the 12 criminal counts it faced, including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets, and conspiracy to defraud the United States. However, the jury acquitted Huawei of a more serious racketeering allegation — a decision Huawei welcomed on Wednesday, stating that the acquittal 'confirms that these allegations lack factual basis.' The original indictment also accused Huawei of attempting to recruit employees of U.S. telecommunications firms and obtaining technological information from them; according to the indictment, this data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to its competitors' while selling at lower prices.

items.summary: A US federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Chinese technology company Huawei Technologies Co. on Tuesday of 10 of the 12 criminal charges it faced, including conspiracy to steal trade secrets and defrauding banks about its business in Iran, while acquitting it of a racketeering charge and obstruction of justice, according to the Department of Justice (DOJ). The verdict came after roughly four days of deliberation in what prosecutors described as a rare prosecution of a foreign corporation. US Attorney General Todd Blanche stated that "no person or company is above the law" and accused Huawei and three subsidiaries of conducting business on "lies and theft," while Assistant Attorney General Tysen A Duva said the verdict signaled America's commitment to defending its businesses, workers, and national security against corrupt foreign corporations. Prosecutors alleged Huawei attempted to recruit employees from US telecom firms to obtain technological information that would let it develop similar products at lower prices, with misappropriated intellectual property reportedly including source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology; prosecutors also claimed the company ran an internal program offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors. The case also involved Huawei's dealings with Iran, where the DOJ said it repeatedly lied about its business by falsely telling banks, journalists, and the US government that it did not assist Iran's government, military, or intelligence community. Huawei now faces potential fines, forfeiture, and restitution, though the US has not specified the scope of financial penalties it will seek. The conviction arrives at a sensitive moment for US-China relations amid ongoing trade tensions; Bloomberg reported the verdict could strain ties further over revelations that Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of links to Chinese intelligence. The case dates back years, including 2022 allegations that two Chinese intelligence officers attempted to bribe a US law enforcement official with $61,000 in Bitcoin to steal evidence and obtain inside information about the case; Huawei has been largely excluded from the American market under trade measures imposed by both Trump and Biden administrations over national security concerns. The company emerged as China's de facto chipmaking champion central to Beijing's goal of dominating artificial intelligence and replacing American software and circuitry with local equivalents, while its CFO Meng Wanzhou was arrested in 2019 at the US's behest on financial fraud charges during a transit through Canada before reaching a deferred prosecution agreement in 2021 that allowed her return to China after admitting the company violated US sanctions by illegally conducting business in Iran.
items.title: US Jury Convicts Huawei of Stealing Trade Secrets, Acquits It of Racketeering

items.summary: US President Donald Trump urged Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang to testify truthfully before Congress next week rather than invoke the Fifth Amendment, which protects individuals from being compelled to give self-incriminating testimony. Speaking in an interview with the New York Post on Tuesday, Trump said he did not believe Huang needed to plead the Fifth over alleged links to a woman suspected of having connections to Chinese intelligence, describing Huang as '100% aboveboard' and adding that his lawyers would advise him on how to approach the questioning. Trump also said he remained open to granting Huang a presidential pardon if necessary but did not think such a step would be required, telling reporters it was 'always an option.' According to CNN, Huang is scheduled to testify behind closed doors before a US Senate committee next Tuesday, followed by a public hearing on Friday, in relation to questions about Nvidia's business dealings with China and compliance with American export restrictions on advanced artificial intelligence chips. The scrutiny has also centered on Huang's acknowledged affair with the Chinese woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, as well as allegations that Nvidia chips may have been diverted to Chinese AI companies through third countries, potentially circumventing US export controls. The hearings are expected to focus on Nvidia's export practices and the national security implications of its business dealings with China.
items.title: Trump Urges Jensen Huang Not to Invoke Fifth Amendment Amid China Scrutiny
